title: Fix the material prompt
scenario: A furniture studio wants an editorial photo of its leather sofa. The brief was written in a hurry and has produced two generic renders in a row — the leather looks plastic and none of the wear the studio loves is visible.
task: Rewrite the prompt so the sofa's material, finish, condition and state each give the model something specific to render.
weakPrompt: a photo of a leather sofa in a nice living room, very premium quality, looks expensive

criteria.label: Names the material precisely
criteria.hint: Full-grain leather? Aniline? Bouclé? “Premium quality” names a price, not a surface.

criteria.label: Describes the finish and sheen
criteria.hint: Matte, satin, oiled, brushed — how does light leave the surface?

criteria.label: Says how worn it is
criteria.hint: Showroom-new or lived-in? Creases on the arms, softened seats, a sun-faded back?

criteria.label: Gives the surface a present state or a light direction
criteria.hint: Dusty, damp, softly lit — texture needs light to appear.

sampleSolution: An editorial photo of a three-seat sofa in cognac leather with an oiled matte finish, a soft sheen along the cushions and gentle worn creases on the arms and seat; a quiet living room with warm afternoon side light raking across the leather from the left.
hints: Replace every judgement with a property: “expensive” becomes a finish, “nice” becomes a material.
Texture hides in flat light — add one clause about how the light meets the surface.
explanation: The weak prompt describes a price and a feeling; the fixed one describes a surface. Cognac, oiled, matte, worn creases: each answer narrows what the renderer can supply, and each is separable — so when the leather looks too new, you adjust one clause instead of the whole brief. Materials reward precision more than any other slot, because everyone recognises how a real surface should age.
